title: Deep lakes, and small cumulus over the forest
summary: Two things the last release said were wrong: lakes froze by the air alone, so deep ones were iced for months too long; and over the Amazon the sky was a few bright clusters where the real afternoon sky is small cumulus everywhere.

sections.name: Lake ice
items: A lake now takes longer to freeze the deeper it is. Lake Constance is iced 6 days a year (it was 57; its record says none), Lake Vättern 13 (it was 55; its record says 13), Lake Tahoe 5.
On lakes the model was not fitted to, it is 10 days a year out on average, from 11. At the 23 recorded lakes large enough to be water in this atlas, what is drawn is 13 days out, from 17.
The north Caspian is 3 m deep and freezes; its middle is 500 m deep and does not. Depth there, and in Baikal and the Great Lakes, is the lake floor itself.

sections.name: Cloud over land
items: By day over warm, wet land a fifth of the cloud's light is now drawn as fields of small cumulus, with a fine structure taken from a real afternoon over the Rio Negro forest. The total light is unchanged.
Against satellite scenes at 2 km: over the Amazon the mean light now matches (0.167 against 0.171), and over the Congo the excess of bright cloud fell from 0.25 to 0.15 of the scene.
Against NASA EPIC, forest between the clouds is nearer its real brightness at three of four places measured, and further at one (the Congo in December).

sections.name: Known to be wrong
items: Lake Mjøsa is still iced 135 days a year against 50: its depth is an estimate, not a measurement. Issyk-Kul, which does not freeze, is iced about 50 days.
Moving light into thin cumulus lowered the whole disc's contrast against EPIC by about one level in 255 in most frames.
Cumulus over the sea does not line up along the wind, and the Amazon still has too few small clouds.
The earlier lists still stand, except where this one says otherwise.

title: The sea where the sea is, and lakes that freeze
summary: The first release said a strip of Hudson Bay was drawn as land. Measured, it was 5.3 million square kilometres of sea, most of it on the Arctic shelf. The coastline is now a coastline, and lakes freeze in winter.

sections.name: Sea and land
items: The East Siberian, Kara and Chukchi shelf seas, south-west Hudson Bay, the mouth of the Amazon, the Yellow Sea and the Bahama banks are sea: they ice over, catch the Sun's glint, and answer a click as water. They had been classed as land since the first build, and went unseen because they were painted in a water colour.
Against an independent survey of the sea floor, sea drawn as land fell from 5.3 to 0.3 million square kilometres. What is left is the coast itself at 5 km: fjords, lagoons, polders.
Shallow and silty water keeps its own colour: the Bahama banks are turquoise, the Amazon's mouth brown, as water.

sections.name: Lake ice
items: Baikal, Great Bear, Great Slave, the lakes of Finland and Tibet, the north Caspian and the Sea of Azov freeze in winter and open in spring. Only the Great Lakes and Ladoga did before.

Outside the Great Lakes and Ladoga the ice is modelled from the air temperature at the lake, and is labelled so. Against the freeze and thaw dates of 83 lakes it was not fitted to, it is 11 days a year out on average. At the lakes it draws, the atlas was 59 days short and is now within 16.

sections.name: Known to be wrong
items: The lake-ice model does not know how deep a lake is. Deep lakes are iced too long: Mjøsa 145 days a year against 50 in its record, Lake Constance 54 against none, Baikal 148 against 102.
Wide rivers are still drawn as lines: the Amazon's main stem is not water.
The first two releases' lists still stand, except the Hudson Bay strip and the lakes that never froze.

title: Cloud that reads as cloud, and a sheet with insets
summary: Two things the first release said were wrong. Close in, cloud was generated and looked it; its fine structure is now taken from satellite photographs of real cloud. And the whole-Earth sheet could not name Central Europe or the small islands of the Caribbean; it now carries an inset for each.

sections.name: Cloud, close in
items: Closer than about 10 km a pixel, cloud now has real cloud's cells, fibres and ragged edges. They come from three satellite scenes at 2 km a pixel: a stratocumulus sheet off Namibia, shallow cumulus in the Indian Ocean and a Southern Ocean storm. How much cloud there is, and how bright, still comes from the climatology.

Against fifteen other satellite scenes, how the atlas's cloud is shared among sizes from 4 to 256 km is nearly three times closer to the photographs than it was, and inside their own day-to-day variation over the North Atlantic, the south-east Pacific and the trades.
Stratocumulus sheets were a third brighter than the satellite record says. Off Peru the scene is now 0.06 above the photographs in reflectance, where it was 0.13.

sections.name: The sheet
items: The whole-Earth sheet has a Europe inset and a Lesser Antilles inset: the same rendered map, magnified three times, with its own names, and every name and country in them opens its card. Poland, Czechia, Hungary, the Baltic states and eight more are named for the first time at this scale, and all eight island states of the Lesser Antilles.

Of the 177 states a reader can see on the sheet at 1440 by 900, 125 are named, where 106 were. The first release said 129: 22 of those names were under the dashboard panel, where no one could read them. Names now keep clear of the panels and move when one opens or closes.
Continent names are back, in wide quiet capitals behind the states.
The insets appear only when there is open sea for them between the panels; in a small window they are left out, not squeezed.

sections.name: Known to be wrong
items: The cloud's fine structure is borrowed: one real sheet stands in for every sheet and one real storm for every storm, and each repeats every 2,000 km. It is not the cloud of the place.
Over the Amazon the real afternoon sky is fine cumulus everywhere; the atlas draws fewer, larger, brighter pieces. Over the Congo it draws twice the bright cloud the photographs show.

Sixteen European states are still unnamed on the whole-Earth sheet, among them Belgium, Switzerland, Denmark and most of the western Balkans; the Levant and the Caucasus have no inset. Zoom in and they are named.
Everything in the first release's list still stands: the Hudson Bay strip, grey snow at a low Sun, the bright outer ring, modelled traffic.

title: First public release
summary: A living atlas of the present-day Earth: one typical year of the planet and its people, composed per pixel, anchored at now. This first release is the state after four rounds of work: a build, a round of measuring it against NASA's photographs, and two rounds of closing what that showed.

sections.name: The Earth from space
items: Colour, exposure, ocean, desert and vegetated land sit within a few display levels of NASA EPIC's full-disc photographs, taken from the same place at the same instant: mean brightness within 2.5 levels in 255.
The ground's colour is Blue Marble re-read against a cloud-free composite of about a hundred EPIC frames. Read the usual way it drew forest and savanna at a third of their brightness.
The limb is as thin as the real air: a scale height of 8 km, where the first build drew a glow 57 and 190 km thick.

sections.name: Cloud and ice
items: How much cloud there is, and how much light it returns, now come from a satellite climatology by kind of cloud. The stratocumulus sheets off Peru, Namibia and California exist; they were all but absent.
Close in, cloud is generated and reads as generated. Where any one cloud is, is not today's weather.

Sea ice is built from NSIDC's own monthly grids for 1991-2020. Its edge is placed where the extent equals NSIDC's mean, so that agreement is by construction; each of the 720 grids on its own converts within 1%.

sections.name: Close in, and names
items: Closer than 5 km a pixel the ground sharpens to about 2 km from tiles fetched while you look (NASA and AWS; see what the page asks the network for).

The whole-Earth sheet names 129 of 198 states, where it named 21. No two names overlap and none sits on another country; Central Europe and the Balkans are too small at that scale and wait for an inset.

sections.name: Known to be wrong
items: A band of shallow south-west Hudson Bay is drawn as land and never ices; lakes other than the Great Lakes and Ladoga never freeze.
The outermost ring of the disc is about 10 levels too bright; snow and sea ice at a low Sun read grey.
Air traffic and ships are modelled flows. No vehicle on screen is a real vehicle.
